titleStmt.title: Interview with Edward Burr II, 23 March 2012
titleStmt.author: Pat Patterson and Paul Lombardi [transcriber]

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Edward Burr II was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

div1.head: Interview with Edward Burr II [23 March 2012]

sp.speaker: Pat Patterson
sp.p: Welcome to Military Memories. I'm Pat Patterson, Lieutenant Colonel US Army retired, and I am the host for today's program. My guest today is Edward Burr, Colonel US Army retired. Welcome to the show, Ed.

sp.speaker: Edward Burr II
sp.p: Hi.

sp.speaker: Pat Patterson
sp.p: For those of you who have been following Military Memories you will recognize Ned Burr because he's been in this chair for quite a number of the programs. This is the last program in the series. So today we are going to give you, Ned, a chance to tell your story. But, with your prior permission, I would like to take just a minute at the start to tribute the producer of military memories Barbara Serage. Barbara has been the power behind this whole program. She set the program up. She made the effort to get accredited by Channel 10. She planned each of the individual segments and, in doing so, Barbara, you have given a lot of people at the Fairfax a chance to tell our stories and be entertained and if having lived with us you know we like to reminisce, by using the good services of Channel 10 you have allowed these stories to be passed out to people who may not even have been alive in World War II and we are providing the tapes to the Library of Congress for their Oral Military History archives. Now, Ned, we have got to get you very quickly into the army and into the war in Europe because this is military memories.

sp.speaker: Edward Burr II
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Pat Patterson
sp.p: You graduated from the United States Military Academy at West Point. You quickly got into the war in Europe. Take it from there.

sp.speaker: Edward Burr II
sp.p: I will. I graduated in 1943 and my first assignment was to the 83rd Infantry Division in Camp Breckinridge, Kentucky. That division was shipped to Europe in late March of 1944 and on the 16th of June received orders that it was to go to France and I landed at Omaha Beach on the 19th of June, which was D plus 13.

sp.speaker: Pat Patterson
sp.p: A little research shows me that D plus 13 was, by civilian language, 13 days after the initial landing, that the beachhead has been pretty well established by then.

sp.speaker: Edward Burr II
sp.p: Oh, yes. I think for the most part if you landed after 2 in the afternoon the beach was fairly safe. We went on from there to relieve the 101st Airborne in Carentan, south of Carentan and on the 4th of July we made an assault with all the American divisions along the line against the Germans to try and break out of Normandy. I'm going to tell my story about that morning of our jump off but basically a lead in from my point of view of the wonderful medical combat support, that combat medical support that was provided by the army to the soldiers along the front line. They saved many lives and one of those lives they saved was mine. When we assembled on the morning of the 4th we moved down a sunken road to get ready to make the attack and we were preceded by a barrage that lasted, oh, probably half an hour, 40 minutes, tremendous barrage of many artillery pieces. When that barrage lifted we started to move forward, but the Germans, who had been digging in for a few days before this, were now coming back out of their holes and returning fire and the fire was extremely intensive. The company commander turned to me, I was a forward observer, that was my role, and at the forward observer role is to direct artillery fire by radio and support of infantry attacks. And he turned to me and said, we need the barrage to start again. So I got with my radioman. We put the radio on, didn't work, I mean, that is, we couldn't make any contact, which was not unusual. They were FM line of sight radios and rarely worked too well, and although my artillery was only located a couple miles behind us we couldn't reach them. So I went with the radioman back up the road, sunken road, and we tried again with no luck and at that point I told him we'll climb up the embankment, which we did which -- one of a number of dumb things that I have done in my career inasmuch as we were now, of course, in direct sight of the German line, even though it was a very, very foggy morning. We set the radio up and at that point I noticed the antenna was stuck in the tree. So I stood up and raised my arm up to fix that situation and the next thing I knew I was back down in the middle of the road and, being knocked down in the middle of the road, I bruised some ribs. So that pain became effective right away. My left arm was stuck up in the air. My only thought at that point was to get back up on the side of the road and see how the radioman was, which I did. As I went to attend to him, because he was bleeding, I realized that I was in deep trouble and as a result of that I began to make my way back along the side of the road as best I could, not entirely in a complete clear frame of mind. What had happened to me was that a fragment of a shell which had landed right by us about the size of a 50-cent piece had entered me through underneath my left armpit and had exited my body just below the shoulder. As I learned later it didn't hit anything but I was losing an enormous amount of blood at that point and had I not got that fixed fairly soon I probably was going to bleed to death right there. So I did have one lucky aspect to this event which was that in the morning when we moved out I, along with everybody else, picked up a couple of hand grenades and hung them off of the shoulder straps of my jacket but somewhere walking down that sunken road to begin with I became very nervous. I don't know why. I took them off and placed them on the side of the road and went on my way. As it turned out, of course, the fragment that went through my left side would have hit the hand grenade hanging off my left shoulder strap for sure. Anyway, I got back along the side of the road and found a little path, a ramp going back down into that road itself and stumbled down that and fortunately bumped into my wire team which had stayed behind. That's about the last thing I remember. I told them about my radio operator and they carried me back to the battalion aid station. These battalion aid stations had a doctor in them, had trained with the infantry and all on the time before the boys got into the business of fighting. Whatever he did, the doctor, to stem the bleeding, I don't know. It was sufficient to bring it to a halt. I was placed in an ambulance and I remember coming to. By the way, morphine was used extensively. I think I was kept on it for pretty much the next two weeks and it pretty well knocks you out, but I did come to in the ambulance to realize I was in it. The ambulance in turn took me to an evacuation hospital. That hospital is basically a major operating hospital, operating, in the case of Normandy, very close to the front line. So I didn't have a long trip back there. Having returned to that hospital, being taken back to it, they operated on the wound. I guess cleaned it out, sewed it up, both front and back, and I was then moved into a ward with a large number of tents in it and again in that ward I would say from the disaster inasmuch as from about the second I was there I spoke to the nurse about feeling very uncomfortable, wet, and the nurses doing what they did so damn well turned me over and I was -- the sutures on the back of the wound had all stripped clean and I was bleeding again severely from the wound. So the nurse in effect saved my life at that stage of the game. From there, after spending about ten days in that hospital, I was moved. I was going to be moved to England and to do that I was put on a stretcher, taken to the beach on I think it was Utah and all of us that were going on the hospital ship were on the beach in stretchers. The only recollection I remember of that is I had to go to the bathroom terribly. Somehow the morphine kicked in again and I forgot all about it until we were taken by a landing craft, an LCT probably, out to the hospital ship and lifted on board and the next time I woke up I was in a very fine bed on board this ship. I don't remember much about the trip back to England on the ship but I do know that we went in to a holding area near the port, probably overnight, until we could be placed on board a train the next day and the train took us then to a general hospital, which was in my case located near Cheltenham, England, and I basically was improving every day that I was there. They didn't have much to do with me except let the wound recover and for me to get better which it did finally around the first of September and I was turned loose, told to return to my outfit.

sp.speaker: Pat Patterson
sp.p: The policy, as I recall, was to try to get you back to the original outfit. Did you make it back to the 83rd?

sp.speaker: Edward Burr II
sp.p: Yes, I did. They carried it out beautifully and, of course, it was terribly important for us, if we could, to go back to our old outfit where we had friends and people we knew. The 83rd when I rejoined it was on the Loire River it moved from the Loire River to Luxembourg and then in early December it moved into Hurtgen Forest to replace the 4th Div and continue that fight. That was a miserable place, the Hurtgen Forest, and then we moved across the Loire River to the Rhine, across the Rhine River north of the Loire valley. We proceeded at a really rapid pace, maybe 20, 25 miles a day from there, until we reached the Elbe River, and we crossed the Elbe River and there wasn't any opposition and we could have probably moved on very quickly and easily to the outskirts of Berlin but, of course, Joe Eisenhower decided that he did not want the American troops involved in that fight which turned out to be one really nasty fight. So that's where I ended the war.

sp.speaker: Pat Patterson
sp.p: Well, you got off to a rough start but you got back in time to get into a lot of it. The war ended while you were on the Elbe River, right?

sp.speaker: Edward Burr II
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Pat Patterson
sp.p: So now the big planners in Washington are concentrating on the invasion and the defeat of Japan and think taking a few of the old line divisions back to train for that. Then all of a sudden in, what, August of that summer, after the second Atom bomb, Japan surrendered.

sp.speaker: Edward Burr II
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Pat Patterson
sp.p: Now the war's over. I suspect that the people in Europe at that time were figuring, how do I get home? How do I get out? And how do I resume a normal civilian life?

sp.speaker: Edward Burr II
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Pat Patterson
sp.p: Did you get caught up in that?

sp.speaker: Edward Burr II
sp.p: No. It's as though somebody called fire and when that war ended everybody headed for the exits. But, no. I was a regular army officer. So I was destined to stay on which I did for another year, approximately. I stayed until March of '46 and finally got an R and R to come home, met the gal I had been writing to for two years or so and -- Marvelous Nikki Bum Bum, and we were married -- no, we weren't. We were engaged at that point. I had to go back for six months and I came back in December of '46 and later in that month we were married.

sp.speaker: Pat Patterson
sp.p: Okay. Now the war to end all wars had been fought and won and the UN was going to take care of all of our problems after that. The army had been reduced a great deal in scale.

sp.speaker: Edward Burr II
sp.p: Yes, it sure has.

sp.speaker: Pat Patterson
sp.p: And we are going to have peace ever after, maybe. I have to go back just a minute. When the Japanese surrendered, they had occupied Korea?

sp.speaker: Edward Burr II
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Pat Patterson
sp.p: And when they surrendered Korea was divided along the 38th Parallel, North Korea and South Korea. North Korea was communist; South Korea wasn't. So they were our friends. Now, we want to get you back in your second war. In the summer, I think it was in June of 1950.

sp.speaker: Edward Burr II
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Pat Patterson
sp.p: The North Koreans attack South.

sp.speaker: Edward Burr II
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Pat Patterson
sp.p: They didn't give any warning and our intelligence didn't give any warning. We were in trouble. How did you get involved in that war?

sp.speaker: Edward Burr II
sp.p: Well, I was in -- when the war broke out I was at Fort Sill attending the advance course which, of course, they cut short right away. We got our orders where we were going to go in probably January of '51. My orders involved going to Korea. My stay at that time, there were only seven of us out of a class of 155 that were sent to Korea. So I went to Korea in March of '51, had joined the 25th Division but what's interested me so much recently has been the support concerns over the families that are left behind in our present wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and the concerns over them and efforts being made all the time to try and give them adequate support. In our case, for those that went to Korea, we really were on our own. I had a two and a half year old daughter, Nikki and our daughter. Decided to resettle her in Levittown, Long Island, near her sister. We didn't have any support, family, as such, that we could go to except her sister who was a widow. So she was left in a little Cape Cod cottage in Levittown to fend for herself, which she did very well. She got a job to help supplement the income, which wasn't the best in the world in those days. But she had some enormously fine experiences but to show you the extent at which the war was becoming an unknown to American people, she went to a party while she was there fairly early on and at the party some woman addressed her about where her husband was and Nikki told her that I was in Korea and the woman looked at her and said, what? Korea? What in the world is he doing in Korea? So that is a pretty good indication that -- oh, it also only appeared on about the 18th page of The New York Times when it was being reported. But she did get some good support in that she's not a bookkeeper. She really hates numbers. So maintaining the bank balance became a major problem for her and to the extent that she finally wrote the Army National Bank to which we belong to The Department of Utter Confusion and stating that she was in this imponderable position and got this marvelous letter back from what the army knew was, Dear Mr. Parker, who was the president of the Army National saying, Dear, little Mrs. Burr, don't worry about a thing. We'll take care of you. No matter what you do it will come out right. So that was a worthwhile -- from a poignancy point of view that thing that really hit home was that she was with her sister during Christmas that year and the two of them had decorated the tree and were proceeding up the stairway, having finished the decorations, to admire it, turn to it and admire it and, as they watched it, the tree slowly but surely fell flat on its face and these two women -- Nikki's sister had lost her husband during the -- in the Pacific during World War II -- simply sat down on the stairs and broke into tears. It was just too much for both of them. At any rate, I did get back a year later in '52, in the spring, and picked the family up in Levittown and we moved to Drexel Hill, Pennsylvania. I was going to attend the University of Pennsylvania for a couple of years. We had been there for, oh, maybe a couple of weeks or so I guess and her sister came to visit and they occupied our bedroom. We slept in the living room and I got up in the early morning to go in the bathroom and Nikki suddenly heard this huge thump and came into the bathroom and I had fainted and fallen into the bathtub. I was completely in the bathtub with my head under the faucet. Now, you know, that's a stunning impact on a young woman married four years, her husband just now flat out in the tub and for all she knows dead. But Nikki had worked five years before we were married. She supported herself from the time she was 17. She was a very competent individual. I don't know what she did exactly but we, of course, had no contacts. There was no 911. She got on the phone and called the United States Army and within about 20 minutes an army doctor appeared at the apartment and determined that I was exhausted and I just simply -- my body had finally given in to exhaustion. And that comes probably from my assignment in Korea where I was a fire direction chief for about 18 -- well, not about, 18 105-millimeter howitzers in the punch bowl the last three months and working about 16 or 18 hours a day. We worked all day long firing on targets of opportunity with this good bit of fire power. And then at night, even after I turned in, I'd get called almost every night at 2 or 2:30 because the Chinese set patrols up to test the water and my foreign observers, and I had nine of them, all had defensive fires laid out in front of them and they would pick a place where they thought these people were coming and open fire and, in addition to that, I had a flu, attack of the flu. So when I got home I lost a considerable amount of weight, was exhausted and that's probably a pretty good explanation as to why I passed out that morning in the bathroom.

sp.speaker: Pat Patterson
sp.p: Well, we are glad the army got you out of the tub anyway.

sp.speaker: Edward Burr II
sp.p: Yes, he did, and he put me in bed and I slept 18 hours with an occasional waking to eat something.

sp.speaker: Pat Patterson
sp.p: Well, Ned, you continued your military career. You retired after 30 years probably as a full colonel. Now you are at the Fairfax where we have lots of time to reminisce. Thinking back over the two wars and the, I think you said once, that you had been in eight major campaigns.

sp.speaker: Edward Burr II
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Pat Patterson
sp.p: In two wars.

sp.speaker: Edward Burr II
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Pat Patterson
sp.p: Thinking back over, how do you visualize World War II and the Korean war looking back from today?

sp.speaker: Edward Burr II
sp.p: Well, for those of us who were in both of them I probably am echoing the sentiments of everyone in that category in that World War II was a very exciting war, exciting in the sense of the whole country was involved. It was energy everywhere when you went. When you traveled on a train during that time frame the camaraderie all through the whole night on a train of families and soldiers, sailors, marines, all moving from one place to another was very solid and very warm. So in a sense the nation was abuzz with excitement about this. Now, I speak with some reservation about the excitement of war, well, it was exciting. For example, for all these millions of young people leaving areas where they normally would have grown up and lived all their lives suddenly to find themselves in strange foreign places and involved in a very exciting activity. And that's where I really, say -- of course, exciting unless you were right smack in the middle of it.

sp.speaker: Pat Patterson
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Edward Burr II
sp.p: And certainly not exciting for the families who lost loved ones and there were 400,000 men and some women killed in that war. So there was a lot of tragedy throughout it all. But overall, again, since the nation in itself didn't suffer from any attack, it suffered no physical involvement in this war. It did work and contribute and there were penalties that were paid by people, rationing and -- on almost everything. So almost everybody in the country had some impact on them because of this war.

sp.speaker: Pat Patterson
sp.p: And how does that compare to Korea?

sp.speaker: Edward Burr II
sp.p: Well, Korea I already explained in part by my wife running into this woman didn't know what Korea was all about, was a first of a number of wars that we have now been engaged in where we send soldiers to do it, we send our military force into the middle of it, but the rest of the country proceeds apace without really any impact whatsoever. There are no requirements for any contributions or for them to do anything and the stories fall off the front page and they lose their visibility and as a result they are sort of unknown and I know the Vietnamese people coming back from that war felt really neglected by the country. But so did the Korean people coming back. I think for some reason in the Korean war we were more adjusted to the idea that it was our job, although for many of the people who went over there, inactive reservists and reservists, it wasn't really their job. They didn't mean to stay that close to the military so they got pulled back into it again. So I think there was a big difference in Korea and, again, I think that difference has played out in recent wars much the same. We are doing, I think, a lot better now with the Afghanistan situation.

sp.speaker: Pat Patterson
sp.p: Well, Ned, you have sat in this chair and looked at the time clock up there a number of times. You know we are running out of time. I want to thank you, very much, for teaching me how to be the host and for being a very interesting and very articulate guest on the program. This is the last -- we are closing out this segment, but this is the last segment in a program. Would you like to close it up for me in 38 seconds?

sp.speaker: Edward Burr II
sp.p: Well, I do have, and I would echo your thoughts at the beginning of the program about Barbara Serage. I think what she's done has been just tremendous. She did it on her own, her own initiative. Using her own smarts. I think all of the Fairfax and all of the military people who get this military history to listen to it and so forth can be thankful to her for the great job she's done.
